blocks.text: Granting a permission is easy. Almost every system makes that part simple, click allow and move on. The harder part is everything that happens after, keeping track of what you granted, reviewing it later, and taking it away cleanly when it is no longer needed.

Permission management is that whole lifecycle. It covers how a grant gets created, how it is remembered, how someone can look back and see who allowed what, and how it gets revoked without leaving a mess behind.
This lesson builds directly on the earlier Tool Permissions lesson. There we looked at the moment of approval. Here we look at everything before and after that moment.
1. What a Permission Actually Represents

blocks.alt: A permission moves from request through review, grant, use, and eventual revocation

blocks.text: A permission is not just a yes or no flag sitting somewhere in memory. It is a standing decision, a record that says a specific client or user is allowed to take a specific action.
That record needs an identity behind it, who or what was granted access, an action, what exactly they can do, and a moment in time, when this was decided.

blocks.title: A permission is a decision, not just a switch
blocks.content: Treat every permission as something a person chose to grant, at a specific time, for a specific reason. That framing makes the rest of the lifecycle, reviewing and revoking, much easier to reason about.

blocks.text: 2. Recap: One Time Approval vs Always Allow

The Tool Permissions lesson introduced two kinds of approval. A one time approval covers a single action and then disappears. An always allow decision is persistent and applies to every future matching request.
Permission management is the layer that sits underneath always allow decisions. A one time approval never needs to be tracked long term because it is gone the moment the action finishes.
An always allow decision is different. It sticks around, which means it needs a home, a way to be reviewed, and a way to be taken back.

blocks.text: 3. The Anatomy of a Permission Record
To manage a permission well, you first need to store it as data, not as a vague assumption. A well formed permission record has a handful of fields that answer who, what, when, and by whom.
Notice that revokedAt starts out null. A permission that has never been revoked simply has nothing in that field yet, which makes it easy to check whether a grant is still active.
4. Granting a Permission

blocks.alt: A request for access leads to a granted permission record

blocks.text: Granting is the moment a user says yes to a request, and that yes needs to be written down immediately, not inferred later from logs or guesswork.

items: Capture exactly what is being granted, not a broad catch all action.
Record who made the decision and exactly when it happened.
Store whether this was a one time approval or an always allow decision.
Make the new grant visible somewhere the user can find it again later.

blocks.text: Skipping any of these steps at grant time makes the rest of the lifecycle much harder, because you cannot review or revoke something you never properly recorded.
5. Reviewing Active Permissions
A grant that nobody ever looks at again tends to outlive its usefulness. Reviewing means giving a user or an administrator a simple place to see every permission that is currently active.
A good review view answers three questions at a glance, who has access, what they can do, and how long they have had it.
Notice the review view includes revoked entries too. Seeing what used to be granted is just as useful as seeing what is currently granted.
6. The Audit Trail: Who Granted What and When

blocks.alt: An audit trail records who granted what permission and when

blocks.text: An audit trail is a running history of every grant and every revoke, kept separately from the current state of a permission. It answers questions that show up much later, sometimes months after a decision was made.
Even after a permission is revoked, the fact that it once existed, who approved it, and why, should still be answerable.

blocks.title: Never overwrite audit history
blocks.content: When a permission changes state, add a new audit entry, do not edit or delete the old ones. The value of an audit trail comes entirely from it being complete and untouched.

blocks.text: 7. Why Revocation Has to Be Clean

blocks.alt: A clean revocation removes access immediately with nothing left behind

blocks.text: Revoking a permission sounds simple, flip it off. But a clean revoke has to actually stop the access everywhere it was being used, not just hide the grant from a list somewhere.
A messy revoke leaves cached tokens valid, leaves background jobs still running under the old grant, or leaves the permission still visible to a check that was written against stale data.

items: Mark the permission record itself as revoked, with a timestamp and an actor.
Invalidate any cached decision so the next check reads the fresh state.
Stop any in flight or scheduled action that depended on that permission.
Write an audit entry so the revoke itself is part of the permanent history.

Here is a small example of what a revoke function looks like in practice. It updates the permission record, clears any cache, and writes an audit entry, all in one place so nothing gets missed.
Notice the function checks whether the permission is already revoked before doing anything. That guard keeps a double revoke from writing confusing duplicate audit entries.
9. Checking a Permission Before an Action Runs

blocks.alt: An action only runs after its permission check passes

blocks.text: A grant only matters if something actually checks it before letting an action proceed. That check needs to look at the live state of the permission, not a value that was cached a long time ago.
This check is intentionally small. All the complexity lives in keeping grantedAt, revokedAt, and the cache in sync, not in the check itself.
10. When Access Should Change: Triggers for Revocation
Revocation is not only something a user chooses to do by hand. Several situations should trigger it automatically, or at least prompt a review.

items: A user removes an integration or uninstalls a client entirely.
A client is found to be misbehaving or requesting far more than it needs.
An employee leaves a team and no longer needs the access they were granted.
A security review flags a permission as unused for a long stretch of time.

blocks.text: Building these triggers into the system, rather than relying purely on someone remembering to check, is what keeps a permission list from quietly growing stale.
11. Stale Permissions and Why They Accumulate

blocks.alt: Unused permissions accumulate over time into stale grants

blocks.text: Left alone, permission lists only ever grow. Nobody feels urgency about revoking something that is not currently causing a problem, so old grants pile up unnoticed.
A permission granted a year ago for a tool nobody uses anymore is still a live door into a user's data, even if nobody is walking through it right now.

blocks.title: Unused does not mean harmless
blocks.content: A stale but active permission is still a working grant of access. The fact that it has not been used recently does not shrink the risk it represents, it just makes the risk easier to forget.

blocks.text: 12. Periodic Review as a Habit
The best defense against stale permissions is a regular review, not a one off cleanup. A short, repeated look at the active permission list catches problems long before they turn into an incident.

items: Look at every permission with an always allow decision type first.
Ask whether the client or integration behind each one is still in active use.
Revoke anything that no longer has a clear, current reason to exist.
Note the review itself in the audit trail, even when nothing changes.

blocks.text: 13. Designing the Data Model for the Lifecycle
A permission management system usually needs two related pieces of storage, the current state of each permission, and a separate append only audit log of every event that touched it.

blocks.text: Keeping these separate means the current state can stay simple and fast to check, while the audit log can grow as large as needed without slowing anything down.
14. Handling Multiple Grants for the Same Client

A single client is often granted more than one permission over time, read access first, then write access later, then something else entirely. Each of these should be its own record, not one record with a growing list of actions bolted on.
Treating each grant as its own row makes revocation precise. You can take away write access to a calendar without touching that same client's permission to read contacts.
15. Scoping Permissions Narrowly

blocks.alt: A narrowly scoped permission is compared against a broadly scoped one

blocks.text: A permission is easier to manage when it covers a small, specific action rather than a broad category. A narrow scope also makes review and revocation far less risky.
Compare a permission scoped to read_calendar_events against one scoped to full_calendar_access. The narrow one tells a reviewer exactly what is at stake, the broad one hides it.

items: Prefer a permission per action, not one permission covering many actions at once.
Name each scope clearly enough that a non technical user can understand it during review.
Avoid catch all scopes like admin or full_access unless there is truly no narrower option.

blocks.text: 16. Notifying a User When Access Changes
A grant or a revoke should rarely happen silently. Letting a user know when their data was accessed under a new grant, or when a permission was removed, builds trust in the whole system.
This does not need to be a heavy notification for every single event. A short summary, delivered at a sensible interval, is often enough to keep a user informed without overwhelming them.

blocks.title: Silence is what makes stale access dangerous
blocks.content: A user who is never reminded what they have granted has no reason to ever go revoke anything. A light, occasional nudge keeps the whole lifecycle honest.

blocks.text: Worked Example: A Permission From Grant to Revoke
Walk through a single permission from the moment it is requested to the moment it is revoked, seeing exactly what gets written at each step.
A user connects a new expense reporting assistant and it asks to submit expense reports on their behalf. The user chooses always allow.
Three months later, the user stops using that assistant entirely and opens their permission review page.
From this point on, any check against perm_9120 returns not active, and the audit log holds a complete record of both the original grant and the later revoke.
Common Mistakes

items: Deleting a permission record on revoke instead of marking it revoked, which destroys the audit trail along with it.
Checking a cached copy of a permission instead of the live record, so a revoke does not actually take effect right away.
Storing one time approvals in the same long lived table as always allow grants, cluttering the list with entries that never needed tracking.
Never reviewing active permissions until something goes wrong, instead of on a regular schedule.
Granting broad, vague actions instead of specific ones, which makes both review and revocation much harder later.
Forgetting to invalidate in flight work when a permission is revoked, so an already running job finishes anyway.

blocks.text: Practice
Design a small permission table for a note taking assistant that can read notes and, separately, delete notes. Give each action its own permission record rather than combining them.

items: Write out the grantedAt, revokedAt fields for both permissions after the user grants read access but denies delete access.
Write a revoke function call that removes only the read permission, leaving nothing else behind for that client.
Sketch what a single audit log entry would look like for that one revoke.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

Granting a permission is only the first step. Real permission management means remembering what was granted, giving people a clear way to review it, and revoking it cleanly the moment access should change.
An audit trail that is never edited, only appended to, is what makes all of that trustworthy months or years later.
